content.text: The law of conservation of energy is one of the most fundamental principles in physics. It tells us that energy cannot be created or destroyed—it can only be transferred from one store to another or transformed from one type to another. This principle underlies all of physics.
The Law of Conservation of Energy
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores or transformed from one type to another.
The total energy in a closed system remains constant
Energy that "disappears" from one store must appear in another
is one where no energy enters or leaves.
In reality, perfectly closed systems don't exist
We often treat systems as closed for simplicity
Accounting for all energy transfers shows energy is conserved
A 2 kg ball is dropped from 5 m. What is its speed just before hitting the ground? (Ignore air resistance, g = 10 m/s²)
A roller coaster car (500 kg) starts from rest at height 30 m and reaches the bottom of a dip at height 5 m. What is its speed? (Ignore friction)
A spring (k = 400 N/m) compressed by 0.1 m launches a 0.2 kg ball. What speed does the ball reach?
A 50 kg skier starts from rest at the top of a 100 m slope. At the bottom, their speed is 30 m/s instead of the expected 44.7 m/s. How much energy was dissipated by friction?
A pendulum is released from height 0.2 m above its lowest point. What is its maximum speed?
At the lowest point, all GPE has converted to KE:
occurs when energy spreads out into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, making it less useful.
Energy is not lost—it's transferred to thermal stores
The energy becomes spread out and harder to use
This is why perpetual motion machines are impossible
Friction converts kinetic energy to thermal energy
Electrical resistance converts electrical energy to heat
While energy is conserved, it tends to spread out and become less useful over time. This is related to the second law of thermodynamics and the concept of entropy.

In energy conservation problems, start by identifying the energy stores before and after the event. Set them equal (for a closed system) and solve for the unknown. Mass often cancels out in falling object problems.

attrs.alt: Pendulum and roller coaster energy conservation: GPE is maximum at the highest points and KE is maximum at the lowest point, with total energy remaining constant

content.text: Maximum height: all GPE, zero KE
Lowest point: zero GPE (relative), maximum KE
Total mechanical energy constant (if no air resistance)
Each bounce loses some energy to sound and heat
Ball doesn't return to original height
Energy is conserved—it goes to thermal and sound stores
At any height: KE = initial KE - GPE gained
Kinetic energy may not be conserved (inelastic collisions)
"Lost" KE goes to thermal, sound, and deformation energy
Electric cars convert KE back to electrical energy when braking
Instead of wasting energy as heat, it's stored in the battery
Water's GPE converts to KE as it falls
KE spins turbines to generate electricity
Energy is conserved at each stage (with some losses)
Mass can be converted to energy: E = mc²
Tiny mass loss = enormous energy release
Machines that run forever without energy input
Any design that claims otherwise violates conservation laws

Energy is always conserved, but it is not always useful. Dissipated energy has spread into the surroundings as thermal energy and cannot easily be recovered. This is why perpetual motion machines are impossible.
— Energy is never used up, only transferred to other stores (often thermal in surroundings).
"Heavier objects fall faster because they have more energy"
— Speed in free fall doesn't depend on mass (
). Heavier objects have more energy but the same speed.
"Perpetual motion is possible with zero friction"
— Even with zero friction, any energy extracted for useful work must come from somewhere.
— Energy can be wasted (dissipated) but never lost. The total remains constant.
— Heat is a transfer mechanism. The store is thermal energy.
Calculate the speed of a 5 kg ball just before it hits the ground after being dropped from 10 m. (g = 10 m/s²)
Calculate the maximum speed of a child on a swing who reaches a maximum height of 0.8 m above the lowest point.
A spring (k = 500 N/m) is compressed by 0.08 m and releases a 0.04 kg ball. a) Calculate the EPE stored in the spring. b) Calculate the speed the ball reaches.
Calculate the maximum height a roller coaster car (mass 400 kg) can reach if it is travelling at 15 m/s at the bottom of a hill. (Ignore friction)
A 60 kg skier starts at rest and descends 50 m. They reach the bottom at 25 m/s. a) Calculate the expected speed without friction. b) Calculate the energy dissipated by friction.
Explain why a bouncing ball eventually stops bouncing, even though energy is conserved.
A 0.5 kg ball is thrown upward at 20 m/s. a) Calculate its total mechanical energy. b) Calculate the height at which its speed will be 10 m/s.
Conservation of energy: Energy cannot be created or destroyed
Total energy before = total energy after (in a closed system)
Energy is often dissipated (spread out as thermal energy)
Dissipated energy is not lost, just less useful
All energy transformations conserve total energy

— v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.8) = sqrt(16) = 4 m/s (calculation)

Each time the ball bounces, some kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy (heating the ball and the ground) and to sound energy. Although total energy is conserved, the useful mechanical energy (KE + GPE) decreases with each bounce because energy is dissipated to the surroundings. Eventually all the mechanical energy has been transferred to thermal energy and the ball stops.
